skills.name: Relate the frequency of a vibrating string to its length, mass per unit length and tension

note.text:
The fundamental frequency of a stretched string depends on three things:
• Length L: f is inversely proportional to L. Halving the length doubles the frequency.
• Mass per unit length µ: f is inversely proportional to √µ. A thicker, heavier string gives a lower note.
• Tension T: f is proportional to √T. Tightening the string raises the note.
Together: f = (1/2L)√(T/µ).
This is why a guitarist presses a string against a fret (shorter L, higher note), why the low strings are thick, and why a string is tuned by turning a peg to change the tension.
The sonometer is the laboratory instrument used to check these relations.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text:
By the end, you should be able to say how the frequency of a vibrating string depends on its length, tension and mass per unit length, and use the formula for its fundamental frequency.
Builds on: Lesson {12} (stationary waves on a string) and Lesson {13} (pitch and frequency).
Leads to: the tuning of musical instruments, and resonance in Form Five.

sections.heading: Three things that change the note
sections.text:
A stretched string sounds its fundamental, with one loop and λ = {2}L.
• Length L: f is inversely proportional to L. Halve the vibrating length and the frequency doubles, so the note rises by an octave. That is what a guitarist does by pressing a string against a fret.
• Tension T: f is proportional to √T. To double the frequency, the tension must be made {4} times as great. A string is tuned by turning a peg to change T.
• Mass per unit length µ: f is inversely proportional to √µ. A thick, heavy string vibrates more slowly, which is why the low strings of a guitar are the thickest.

sections.heading: The formula and the sonometer
sections.text:
Putting the three together:
f = ({1} ÷ {2}L) × √(T ÷ µ).
The same result follows from v = fλ: for the fundamental λ = {2}L, so f = v ÷ ({2}L), and the speed of the wave on the string depends on T and µ.
A sonometer is used to check these relations in the laboratory: a wire is stretched over two bridges by a known weight, and the bridges are moved to change the vibrating length. Keeping two of the three quantities fixed and changing the third shows each relation in turn.

examples: half the length → double the frequency
{4} times the tension → double the frequency

mistake.wrong: doubling the tension doubles the frequency
mistake.right: the tension must be {4} times as great
mistake.why: f is proportional to the SQUARE ROOT of the tension, and √{4} = {2}.

worked_example.problem: A string of length L vibrates at {f1} Hz. It is pressed down so that only {1}/{k} of its length can vibrate, with the tension unchanged. Find the new frequency.
steps: Frequency is inversely proportional to the vibrating length: f ∝ {1}/L.
The length is divided by {k}, so the frequency is multiplied by {k}.

cards.idea: f is inversely proportional to the length: halve the length and the frequency doubles.
example: {200} Hz on a full string becomes {400} Hz on half of it

cards.idea: f is proportional to √T: to double the frequency the tension must be {4} times as great.

check.prompt: A string vibrates at {f1} Hz. The tension is increased to {k * k} times its old value, with the length and the string unchanged. Find the new frequency, in hertz.

misconceptions.explain: The frequency goes with the SQUARE ROOT of the tension: × {k}, not × {k * k}.
A tighter string gives a HIGHER note.

solution: √{k * k} = {k}, so the frequency is multiplied by {k}.

cards.idea: f is inversely proportional to √µ: a thicker, heavier string gives a lower note.

check.prompt: A string vibrates at {f1} Hz. It is replaced by one of the same length and tension but with {k * k} times the mass per unit length. Find the new frequency, in hertz.

misconceptions.explain: A heavier string gives a LOWER note.
Use the square root of the mass per unit length: ÷ {k}, not ÷ {k * k}.

solution: √{k * k} = {k}, so the frequency is divided by {k}.

questions.prompt: A string {L} cm long gives a note of {f1} Hz. The vibrating length is changed to {L2} cm, with everything else the same. Find the new frequency, in hertz.

misconceptions.explain: A SHORTER string gives a HIGHER note: f is inversely proportional to L.
Changing the vibrating length changes the frequency.

solution: f is inversely proportional to L, so f₁L₁ = f₂L₂.

pick.q: presses a string against a fret nearer the middle of the neck
pick.r: It becomes higher, because the vibrating length is shorter
pick.w1: It becomes lower, because the string is shorter
pick.w2: It becomes louder but keeps its pitch
pick.y: f is inversely proportional to the vibrating length, so a shorter length gives a higher frequency.

pick.q: turns a peg to tighten a string
pick.r: It becomes higher, because the tension is greater
pick.w1: It becomes lower, because the string is stretched
pick.w2: It becomes louder but keeps its pitch
pick.y: f is proportional to √T, so more tension gives a higher frequency.

pick.q: plays the thickest string instead of the thinnest, at the same length and tension
pick.r: It is lower, because the mass per unit length is greater
pick.w1: It is higher, because a thick string carries more energy
pick.w2: It is the same, because the length is the same
pick.w3: It is louder but the same pitch
pick.y: f is inversely proportional to √µ, so a heavier string gives a lower frequency.

pick.q: plucks the same string harder, changing nothing else
pick.r: It is louder, with the same pitch
pick.y: Plucking harder increases the amplitude, which changes the loudness; the frequency is set by L, T and µ.

questions.prompt: A guitarist {act}. What happens to the note?
A string of vibrating length {L} m carries a wave of speed {v} m/s. Find its fundamental frequency, in hertz.

misconceptions.explain: For the fundamental the wavelength is {2}L, not L.

solution: For the fundamental, λ = {2}L = {2} × {L} = {2 * L} m.
